newsitem.title: CROATIA: On election eve, Croatia refugee attitudes hard.
newsitem.headline: On election eve, Croatia refugee attitudes hard.

text.p: A day before Croatia's first nationwide elections, attitudes towards Serbs living in the east of the country were as hard as ever and politicians' promises of reconciliation seemed optimistic.

In the city of Osijek, in sight of the front line of Croatia's 1991 war for independence from former Yugoslavia, thousands of Croat refugees who fled Serb attacks swear they will never live side by side with their former enemies.

Even local politicians admit reintegrating Eastern Slavonia into Croatia could take far longer than originally promised. The region is now populated almost entirely by Serbs, including thousands of refugees from elsewhere in Croatia and Bosnia.
Around 26,000 displaced live in Osijek. The splendid old Austro-Hungarian town with wide avenues and squares has an air of faded grandeur and is enclosed on three sides by Eastern Slavonia.
Just outside the town boundary lies a sprawling refugee camp -- home to 2,600 people. Prefabricated huts stand in neat rows with satellite dishes sprouting from their roofs.
Outside many of the huts refugees have cultivated gardens with daffodils, apple trees and vegetable plots -- proof that this former field has been home to hundreds for six years now.

Katica Vlahovic, 58, is one of the refugees who plans to move back to her home in Eastern Slavonia after Sunday's municipal elections and like virtually all the others will vote for President Franjo Tudjman's conservative nationalist HDZ.

"I don't want to see a single Serb in my village. None of them are good, they're all the same. They may continue to live there but they won't rule again...We want the HDZ to lead us so we can once again plough our fields and start sowing."
She said the Serb living in her house had removed all her belongings. "We hear he keeps saying none of this is his fault but in fact he emptied our house.
"I'm truly glad we are going home now and he's welcome to wait there," she shouted to cheers from onlookers.

Vlado Kupina, a tiny 84-year-old man with gaping teeth and a glass eye, said he would go back to his village but it was hard to say if he could live with the Serbs. "They torched our homes, killed our people and threw us in the streets."
He lifted his cap to show a scar on his forehead. "They beat me with their rifles and kicked me. I lost my left eye and this is made of glass. I am still weak from those beatings."
Only one woman showed no hatred for Serbs. Knitting in the sunshine beside a strawberry plot by her house, she said she was looking forward to living with former neighbours.
"We've met our Serb neighbours twice. They are our closest friends and they've proved to be very good people who helped us a lot through all this."

Branimir Glavas, HDZ regional prefect, said it could take months before Eastern Slavonia comes under Croatian government control. The mandate of United Nations troops administering the region expires on July 15.

"It would not be a tragedy if the whole process lasted until the autumn. I believe they should be able to go back to their homes, and the Croatian government should be reinstated, before the winter," he told Reuters. He believed the majority of Serbs will stay in the region after reintegration.

Mato Simic, the hardline chairman of the Croatian refugee association, was less charitable. "Politics is one thing and life is another. The wish of the politicians and the reality on the ground are quite different."
